blocks.content: docker run is the single most-used Docker command, it creates a new container from an image and starts it, in one step.

Under the hood, docker run is really docker create followed immediately by docker start. Knowing this makes the rest of the container lifecycle commands easier to reason about, they are the same underlying operations, just invoked separately.
2. The Flags You Will Use Constantly
blocks.text: 2. The Flags You Will Use Constantly

blocks.content: A handful of flags cover the overwhelming majority of real usage: -d to run detached in the background, -p to map a host port to a container port, -v to mount a volume, and --name to give the container a memorable name instead of a random one.

blocks.alt: A small set of flags covers most real usage

blocks.content: Put together, a realistic docker run invocation reads naturally once you know what each flag does: run this image, in the background, reachable on this host port, under this name.

blocks.alt: Every flag adds one specific behavior

blocks.content:
docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx
# -d: detached, runs in background
# -p 8080:80: host port 8080 maps to container port 80
# --name web: this container is now addressable as "web"

code.content:

blocks.content: 4. Where It Sits in the Bigger Picture
blocks.text: 4. Where It Sits in the Bigger Picture

blocks.content: Every other lifecycle command (stop, start, rm, and the rest) assumes a container already exists. docker run is the command that actually brings one into existence in the first place.

blocks.alt: Nothing exists until docker run creates it

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker run combines create and start into one command, it is almost always your entry point into a container's lifecycle.
Learn -d, -p, -v, and --name first, they cover the large majority of everyday docker run usage.
